claim_verdicts.evidence: `git -C examples/don-hang show stage-1:DonHang.Infrastructure/DonHangDbContext.cs` lines 9-14 are exactly: `public DbSet<Customer> Customers => Set<Customer>();` `public DbSet<Product> Products => Set<Product>();` `public DbSet<Order> Orders => Set<Order>();` `public DbSet<OrderItem> OrderItems => Set<OrderItem>();` `public DbSet<Payment> Payments => Set<Payment>();` `public DbSet<Notification> Notifications => Set<Notification>();` — six properties, expression-bodied over `Set<T>()`. Tag stage-1 resolves to commit 4fca60a.

refs/efcore-docs/entity-framework/core/index.md: "EF Core can serve as an object-relational mapper (O/RM), which: Enables .NET developers to work with a database using .NET objects."; "A model is made up of entity classes and a context object that represents a session with the database. The context object allows querying and saving data."; "Instances of your entity classes are retrieved from the database using Language Integrated Query (LINQ)."

Verbatim in refs/efcore-docs/entity-framework/core/modeling/entity-properties.md line 30, section "Column names": "By convention, when using a relational database, entity properties are mapped to table columns having the same name as the property." Followed by: "If you prefer to configure your columns with different names, you can do so as following code snippet" with Data Annotations and Fluent API tabs. No built-in snake_case convention exists: extensions/index.md lists EFCore.NamingConventions as a third-party plugin for snake_case naming.

`git show stage-1:DonHang.Domain/Entities.cs` lines 17-22: `public sealed class Product { public int Id { get; set; } public required string Name { get; set; } public int PriceVnd { get; set; } }`. Exactly three properties, no attributes, no base class, no using of Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore in the file (only `namespace DonHang.Domain;`).

Source lines 30-36 are `modelBuilder.Entity<Product>(e => { e.ToTable("products"); e.Property(p => p.Id).HasColumnName("id"); e.Property(p => p.Name).HasColumnName("name"); e.Property(p => p.PriceVnd).HasColumnName("price_vnd"); });`. Same shape as the EF Core docs sample refs/efcore-docs/samples/core/Modeling/EntityProperties/FluentAPI/ColumnName.cs: `modelBuilder.Entity<Blog>().Property(b => b.BlogId).HasColumnName("blog_id");`
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang @ stage-1: DonHangDbContext.cs lines 30-36; refs/efcore-docs samples/.../FluentAPI/ColumnName.cs

issues.text: "fail silently" is wrong and contradicts the lesson's own quiz. With `PriceVnd` unconfigured, EF Core emits SQL against a column named `PriceVnd`; PostgreSQL answers with an error, loudly, at query time. Verified: `psql -c 'select "PriceVnd" from products'` → `ERROR: column "PriceVnd" does not exist / HINT: Perhaps you meant to reference the column "products.price_vnd".` Quiz q5's keyed answer already says "the query fails". This is also an unlisted behaviour claim — no entry in .meta.json claims covers it.
issues.quote: `PriceVnd` is the one that would fail silently without it
issues.fix: Replace with: "`PriceVnd` is the one that breaks without it: left unconfigured, EF Core would ask PostgreSQL for a column literally named `PriceVnd`, and the query would fail at runtime — `column \"PriceVnd\" does not exist` — because the table only has `price_vnd`." Add a `behavior` claim to .meta.json citing the psql run.

issues.text: `ProductsController.List()` never produces a `Product` object. At stage-1 its body is `await db.Products.Select(p => new ProductDto(p.Id, p.Name, p.PriceVnd)).ToListAsync()` — a projection EF Core translates into SQL, so no `Product` instance is materialised there. Yet the lesson anchors its question on that method (§1 "turns those rows into `Product` objects", §2 "a `Product` object it calls `p`"). The method that does materialise a `Product` is `Get(int id)`: `var product = await db.Products.FindAsync(id);` — also the Try it endpoint.
issues.quote: this lesson is about the piece that turns those rows into `Product` objects in the first place
issues.fix: Re-anchor §1 and §2 on `ProductsController.Get(int id)`: `db.Products.FindAsync(id)` returns a `Product` object (the variable is `product`, not `p`), and the controller builds `new ProductDto(product.Id, product.Name, product.PriceVnd)` from it. Drop the claim that `List()`'s `p` is a `Product` object that EF Core built; keep `List()` only as "the endpoint you already saw".

issues.text: Unlisted claim: "a `DbSet<Product>` doesn't hold any `Product` objects until something asks it a question" is a behaviour claim about deferred execution, and nothing in .meta.json's six claims covers it. It happens to be supportable — refs/efcore-docs/entity-framework/core/querying/how-query-works.md: "When you call LINQ operators, you're simply building up an in-memory representation of the query. The query is only sent to the database when the results are consumed." — but the author did not put it in the ledger, so it was never checked.
issues.quote: a `DbSet<Product>` doesn't hold any `Product` objects until something asks it a question
issues.fix: Add a claim to .meta.json (kind `behavior`, version_key `efcore`, section 6) quoting how-query-works.md: "The query is only sent to the database when the results are consumed." Leave the lesson sentence as is.

issues.text: "a standing connection to a table" is inaccurate and contradicts the quiz. A `DbSet<T>` holds no database connection; connections are opened when a query runs and the connection string belongs to the `DbContext`'s options. Quiz q1's explanation for option d says the opposite: "a `DbSet<T>` never holds connection details itself."
issues.quote: a `DbSet<Product>` is a standing connection to a table, holding nothing until asked
issues.fix: Replace with: "a `DbSet<Product>` is a standing question you can ask about a table, holding nothing until it is asked." (No mention of connections.)

issues.text: `DbSet<T>` is a type, not a property; `Products` is the property that exposes it. EF Core docs (modeling/entity-types.md): "types that are exposed in DbSet properties on your context are included in the model as entities". The bullet as written makes `DbSet<T>` itself "a property", which collides with §5's "Each line pairs one entity class with one `DbSet<T>` property".
issues.quote: `DbSet<T>` — a property on the `DbContext` representing one table as a queryable collection of `T` objects
issues.fix: Rewrite the bullet as: "`DbSet<T>` — the type of a property on the `DbContext` that stands for one table as a queryable collection of `T` objects; `DbSet<Product>` stands for the whole `products` table."

issues.text: "unit of work" is a term of art used without definition and is in neither `known_vocab` (tools/known-vocab --before backend.l1.efcore-mapping) nor this lesson's `vocab: [orm]`. It carries real meaning in EF Core (dbcontext-configuration/index.md: "A `DbContext` instance is designed to be used for a _single_ unit-of-work"), i.e. lifetime and change tracking — everything this lesson explicitly does not teach.
issues.quote: the object standing between your code and the database for one unit of work
issues.fix: Drop the phrase: "A `DbContext` is the object standing between your code and the database: you ask its `DbSet<Product>` for data…". If the lifetime idea is wanted later, introduce it in the lesson that owns DbContext lifetime, with a glossary term.
